## Abstract

Emission reductions required to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement have been extensively 45

analyzed using integrated assessment modeling scenarios. However, the contribution of urban areas in aggregate, globally, by region and by city type, remains underexplored. Here, we develop a spatially explicit framework to downscale global emissions pathways to urban areas, differentiated by region and city type. Ambitious climate change mitigation could deliver 21 GtCO₂e of greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reductions in urban areas by 2050 relative to a 50

continuation of current policies and trends, primarily by transitioning away from fossil fuels in electricity and heat supply, deep decarbonization of industry, and mitigation in the transport and buildings sectors. Mitigation potential is concentrated in established and rapidly growing cities, reflecting their high current per-capita emission levels. Asian regions with high urbanization levels dominate global urban emissions and reduction potentials. The findings underscore the central 55

role of cities in achieving global climate targets and highlight the importance of differentiated mitigation strategies across regions and city types.

## 1. Introduction

Cities are central to global climate change mitigation because they concentrate people, economic activity, infrastructure, and energy demand (Seto et al 2014). Urban areas account for roughly 70% 60

of global final energy use and a similar share of energy-related CO₂ emissions, making them critical sites for mitigation action (Lwasa et al 2022). At the same time, cities offer substantial mitigation opportunities across buildings, transport, energy supply (Creutzig et al 2016), and urban form (Creutzig et al 2015). Many of these actions are cost-effective and deliver significant co-benefits such as improved air quality, health, and accessibility (Becvarik et al 2024, Castillo et al 2021, Creutzig et 65

al 2025).

Despite their central role, the evolution of the urban share in global emissions across sectors and city types remains poorly quantified, limiting the ability to align subnational action with national and global climate targets. Scenarios from integrated assessment models (IAMs) have long served as primary tools for exploring emissions futures (Weyant 2017) providing crucial inputs for climate 70

policymaking (UNFCCC 2023, IPCC 2022), financial risk assessment (NGFS 2024, Bertram et al 2021), and Earth system modeling (O’Neill et al 2016, Gidden et al 2019, van Vuuren et al 2025).

However, IAMs have limited geographical resolution and typically represent 12–32 aggregated world regions, lacking the spatial granularity required to capture subnational heterogeneity, including differences between urban and rural energy use and emission patterns. Very few studies use 75

variants of IAMs to analyze city-level emissions directly. Weber et al. (2024) and Waite et al. (2024) implemented the cities of Kuala Lumpur and Bangkok, respectively, as explicit regions in the Global Change Analysis Model (GCAM) to analyze climate change mitigation strategies for these cities. Using an energy system model, Jacobson et al. (2018) derived transformation pathways for US cities. Other studies used IAMs to estimate urban and rural emissions from the transport and residential 80

energy use in selected countries (Yin et al 2015, Krey et al 2012, Daioglou et al 2012). Still others use IAM-derived scenarios to benchmark subnational mitigation efforts against current national policies or to evaluate their aggregate global impact (Kuramochi et al 2020, Hsu et al under review).

However, these approaches do not provide a comprehensive, sector-resolved assessment of the aggregate urban contribution to global emissions across a wide range of mitigation scenarios. 85

Addressing this gap requires downscaling global emissions pathways to the urban scale in a manner that preserves sectoral dynamics and scenario consistency. Downscaling IAM scenarios is an established practice (van Vuuren et al 2010, Grübler et al 2007).  Gurney et al. (2022) combine historical urban per-capita consumption-based CO₂ emissions (Moran et al 2018) with projections from the Shared-Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) to derive urban emission scenarios under 90

alternative socioeconomic developments and global mitigation goals, but do not resolve emissions across sectors or capture sector-specific decarbonization dynamics.

Here, we develop a spatially explicit downscaling framework that links global emissions pathways from the ScenarioMIP–CMIP7 ensemble (van Vuuren et al 2025) with gridded socioeconomic projections and urban settlement patterns. This approach enables the derivation of sector-resolved 95

GHG emission pathways for urban areas, differentiated by world regions and city types. We address three questions: (i) How does the urban contribution to global GHG emissions evolve across sectors under different climate policy scenarios? (ii) How do mitigation potentials vary across regions and city types? (iii) What role do cities play in achieving deep emission reductions consistent with the goals of the Paris Agreement? 100

Our results provide a systematic and sector-resolved perspective on the role of urban areas in global mitigation pathways, offering insights to inform city-level climate strategies, support the alignment of subnational action with national and global targets, and contribute to upcoming assessments such as the IPCC Special Report on Cities and Climate Change.

## 2. Methods

2.1 Global emission scenarios

In ScenarioMIP-CMIP7, seven IAM systems – AIM 3.0 (Hasegawa et al 2017, Fujimori et al 2024), COFFEE 1.6  (Zanon-Zotin et al 2025), GCAM 8s (Calvin et al 2019), IMAGE 3.4 (Stehfest et al 2014) , MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM-GAINS 2.1-M-R12 (Fricko et al 2017, Krey et al 2020, Kishimoto et al 2025), 110

REMIND-MAgPIE 3.5-4.11 (Baumstark et al 2021, Dietrich et al 2019), and WITCH 6.0 (Emmerling et al 2016)  – are used to derive a wide range of plausible emissions futures under different levels of climate policy ambition and alternative assumptions about socio-economic development, energy use, and land use. Socioeconomic development is prescribed based on the narratives and quantitative drivers of the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) (O’Neill et al 2014). 115

Van Vuuren et al. (2025) describe the scenario narratives for the seven illustrative emission and land use futures, ranging from a High emission scenario exploring the upper end of plausible future emissions, to a Very Low emission scenario limiting the overshoot of 1.5°C and returning to below 1.5°C by the end of the century. In view of current country-level backlashes against climate policies and increasing interest in scenarios that study temperature overshoot (Tavoni et al 2026), the 120

scenario set includes several pathways featuring delayed climate action.

The High emission scenario is characterized by a global rollback and eventual collapse of climate policies, the breakdown of international cooperation, and nations increasingly prioritizing economic and security interests over mitigation efforts. The High-to-Low emission scenario follows a similar emissions pathway over the first half of the century, albeit driven by a different narrative based on 125

high growth and rapid technological change. After 2060 it assumes a surge in climate policy ambition aimed at drastically cutting emissions and upscaling carbon dioxide removal. The Medium emission scenario assumes the continuation of existing policies and techno-economic trends. Domestic policy targets such as NDCs and net-zero pledges are not included in this scenario unless a corresponding legislation is in place. The Medium-to-Low emission scenario initially assumes current domestic 130

policies and trends as in the M scenario, but moderately increases climate policy ambition after 2040 to reach net-zero CO₂ globally around the end of the century. The Low emission scenario is consistent with holding warming likely below 2°C, reflecting the NDCs for 2030 and achieving global GHG neutrality by 2100. The Low-to-Negative emission scenario assumes a continuation of current policies and trends until 2035. Strong climate policies thereafter trigger deep emission reductions to 135

rapidly achieve net-zero GHG emissions, relying on large-scale carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies in the second half of the century to limit the duration of the overshoot of 1.5°C. The Very Low emission scenario combines the most ambitious and rapid emission reductions with broad sustainability transformations across all sectors. Its goal is to achieve the lowest plausible peak warming through rapid decarbonization of the electricity supply, deep electrification of energy 140

demand sectors, and behavioral shifts in transportation, consumption, and diets while limiting reliance on large-scale CDR options.

For each of the seven scenario narratives, one scenario quantification by a specific IAM model was selected as a marker scenario (Table 1). In this study, we focus on the seven selected marker scenarios for analyzing urban emission futures. 145

2.2 Downscaling of emission scenarios to urban scale

The method for estimating the urban contribution to future global GHG emissions comprises multiple steps (described in detail in Suppl. Mat. S1): (i) downscaling from native IAM regions to country level and harmonization with historical emissions inventories using a well-established method (Gidden et al 2018); (ii) downscaling from country level to grid level with 0.1°×0.1° grid while 155

accounting for dynamic changes in the subnational distribution of GDP and population; (iii) calculation of urban emissions on national and regional levels based on gridded projections of urban population; and (iv) calculation of urban emissions by city type using the typology introduced by Montfort et al. (2026). These steps are calculated separately for each sector and emission species.

Step (ii) is the central element of this methodology. It downscales aggregate country-level emissions 160

for each sector according to the base year spatial pattern of sector emissions (Hoesly et al 2025) adjusted for projected changes in the spatial pattern of socio-economic drivers: gridded  population (Bondarenko et al 2025a, 2025b) for buildings, transport and waste, and gridded GDP (Paprotny 2025) for energy supply and industry. Resulting gridded emissions are shown in Figure 3a and Supplementary Figures S6-S9. 165

In step (iii), following the degree of urbanization (DEGRUBA) approach (Dijkstra et al 2021) we allocate emissions from each grid cell to (1) cities, (2) towns and suburbs (peri-urban zones), and (3) rural areas in proportion to the population share of each category. Throughout this manuscript, urban emissions refer to the aggregate of emissions from cities plus towns and suburbs. We focus on the energy supply, industry, transport, buildings and waste sectors, for which human settlements are 170

dominant contributors. The analysis considers gross fossil GHG emissions from these sectors, excluding AFOLU and international bunkers.. Wherever reported carbon dioxide removal (CDR)refers to economy-wide deployment including non-urban contributions, since the downscaling method does not allow to distinguish urban from non-urban CDR. In these cases, only permanent CDR is considered, excluding land sinks. 175

The grid-based approach used here differs from approaches that calculate urban emissions within administrative boundaries (Yu et al 2026), although the global urban share in territorial emissions are broadly comparable (Yu et al 2026). Importantly, the territorial emissions analyzed here do not account for emissions related to goods and services consumed in cities but produced outside of cities. This approach differs from consumption-based emissions accounting which uses input-output 180

methods downscaled to urban areas (Moran et al 2018, Gurney et al 2022).

supply, industry, transport, buildings and waste sectors are projected to decline from 29 GtCO₂e in 2025 to 25 GtCO₂e in 2050, stabilizing thereafter. In the High and High-to-Low scenarios, assuming a rollback of climate policies, urban emissions increase to 32-37 GtCO₂e by 2050. Very Low, characterized by high climate policy ambition and sustainability-oriented development, implies a

The development of urban emissions largely reflects the evolution of global GHG emissions in the respective scenarios. We find that urban areas account for 66% of global GHG emissions from the considered sectors in 2025, broadly consistent with studies based on historic inventories (Crippa et al 2021, Yu et al 2026). In Medium, the urban share in global emissions increases gradually to 77% by 195

Global average per capita GHG emissions in urban areas in 2025 are 4.6 tCO₂e/cap, around 20% lower than the global average, and range between 5.0 tCO₂e/cap in High-to-Low and 0.5 tCO₂e/cap in Very Low in 2050 (Figure 2).

3.2 Emission trends and mitigation potentials across sectors 200

Urban areas account for around 67% of GHG emissions from energy supply and 75% of those from industry in 2025. These sectors also hold the largest potential for emissions reductions. While emissions from urban energy installations only decline slightly in Medium, Very Low exhibits a 92% reduction in urban energy supply emissions. Urban industry emissions decline by 82% by 2050 relative to 2025 in Very Low. Residual GHG emissions in deep mitigation scenarios are typically 205

dominated by residual fossil fuel use for bulk material production, such as chemicals, steel and cement (Luderer et al 2022, Zanon-Zotin et al 2025).

Urban areas also dominate direct emissions from the buildings sector, accounting for more than 60% of the sector total; these emissions arise mainly from space and water heating as well as cooking. Importantly, the buildings sector also causes substantial indirect emissions associcated with 210

electricity (e.g., for air conditioning or appliances), district heating and construction materials (Cabeza et al 2022). Under territorial accounting, these emissions are represented in the energy supply and industry sectors. In absolute terms, direct buildings emissions are projected to decrease from around 2.3 GtCO₂e in 2025 to around 1.5 GtCO₂e in 2050 in Medium, and to 0.16 GtCO₂e in Very Low – indicating a substantial mitigation potential from energy-efficiency improvements and 215

the electrification of heating and cooking.

Transport demand includes both short-distance trips that are predominantly urban and linked to population density, and long-distance travel and freight that is also strongly correlated to economic activity (Creutzig et al 2022b, Schäfer et al 2009). Energy use and emissions from transport are therefore more spatially distributed, and urban areas only account for around half of the territorial 220

emissions of this sector (excluding bunkers, i.e. international aviation and shipping). Under a continuation of current climate policy ambition (Medium), urban transport emissions are projected to decrease gradually, as the increasing electrification of road transport offsets the increasing demand, in particular in developing and emerging economies. Even in the High and High-to-Low scenarios with weak climate policies, urban GHG emissions from transport stabilize. By contrast, 225

Very Low shows a near-complete elimination of GHG emissions from transport by 2070, corresponding to emission reductions of 2.0 GtCO₂e/yr compared to Medium.

The treatment of municipal solid waste and wastewater generates GHG emissions – predominantly methane and nitrous oxide  almost 80% of which occur within urban areas. Urban waste emissions

3.4 Urban emissions vary widely across city types 290

To interpret variation in urban GHG emissions across diverse urban systems, we draw on the global city typology developed by Montfort et al. (2026). The typology groups cities with shared characteristics relevant to climate action, thus enabling comparisons among cities facing similar climate-related challenges. It captures the spectrum of urban development (population and population growth, share of population above age 65, population density and its change), 295

socioeconomic development (GDP,GDP growth, and an index of critical infrastructures), and biophysical conditions affecting energy demand (such as heating or cooling requirements). Drawing on existing IPCC nomenclature (Lwasa et al, 2022), we refer to the four types as emerging, rapidly growing, established, and large and megacities. Emerging cities are smaller, lower-income cities with limited infrastructure, low human development, and high cooling needs; rapidly growing cities are 300

economically expanding cities with intermediate infrastructure, low population density, and rapid horizontal growth; established cities encompass wealthier cities with strong infrastructure and limited population and economic growth; and large and megacities are high-density, fast-growing cities with large population and relatively advanced infrastructure but acute cross-sectoral pressures. . Together, these four types cover 69% of urban population, 75% of urban GDP, and 70% of urban GHG emissions 305

in 2025. Within these typologies, established and rapidly growing cities dominate urban GHG emissions in 2025, together accounting for 14 GtCO₂e (Figure 4a). Under Medium, emissions from established and rapidly growing cities decline only gradually, whereas emissions from emerging cities increase over 310

time and eventually exceed those of rapidly growing cities. Hence, without deep mitigation, an increasing share of future urban emissions will come from city types that currently have lower percapita emissions. Under Very Low, by contrast, emissions decline rapidly across all city types, with the largest absolute reductions occurring in established and rapidly growing cities. 315

Per-capita GHG emissions also differ across city types. In 2025, rapidly growing (6.7 tCO₂e/cap) and established cities (6.0 tCO₂e/cap) have the highest per-capita emissions compared with around 2.2– 3.0 tCO₂e/cap in emerging cities and megacities (Figure 4b). The sectoral composition is broadly similar across city types, although rapidly growing cities have relatively larger contributions from energy supply and industry (Figure 4c). Under Medium, per-capita emissions decrease slightly in established, 320

rapidly growing and megacities, but increase modestly in emerging cities. Under Very Low, by contrast, per-capita emissions decline sharply in all city types and converge to below 0.7 tCO₂e/cap by 2050.

4. Discussion and conclusion

Building on a novel sector-detailed downscaling of ScenarioMIP-CMIP7 pathways, our analysis shows that urban areas will account for a dominant and increasing fraction of global GHG emissions, and 335

offer substantial emission reduction potential. Under high climate policy ambition, urban areas can combine for a total of 21 GtCO₂e of GHG emission reductions by 2050 relative to a continuation of current policies and trends, most importantly from transitioning away from fossil fuels for electricity and heat supply, defossilization of industry, and mitigation action in the transportat, buildings and waste sectors. The dominant roles of energy supply and industry indicate that urban mitigation 340

cannot be understood solely through local demand-side interventions in the transport and buildings sectors, but also depends fundamentally on national and global infrastructure transitions. Nonetheless, the demand-side interventions (Creutzig et al., 2022), and especially urban planning (Creutzig et al., 2026), remain important and are areas where municipalities have considerable agency. 345

Urban emissions and emission reduction potentials, both in absolute and in per-capita terms, exhibit pronounced heterogeneity across regions and city types. Asia dominates both current emissions and future mitigation potentials, accounting for around 60% of urban emissions and more than half of the reduction potential. In terms of city types, rapidly growing and established cities hold the largest share in global mitigation potentials. Per-capita emissions levels and mitigation potentials are 350

greatest in fossil-intensive countries of the Middle East, former Soviet Union and China. Urban areas and emerging cities in Africa and parts of Asia are characterized by low per-capita emissions levels. Dedicated climate policies can enable green growth and prevent a replication of emission-intensive structures currently observed in other world regions.

Mitigation requires action across all sectors, world regions and city types. Table 2 illustrates key 355

options for all six sectors, which can facilitate GHG emission reductions (Table 2). Urban planning strategies are particularly relevant for rapidly growing cities and megacities in Asia and Africa (Creutzig et al. 2026). Other strategies, like building retrofit, will be most important for established cities. Although fleet electrification was previously viewed primarily as a strategy for richer OECD countries, energy security concerns and the rapidly declining costs of batteries are accelerating 360

electric vehicle adoption in Chinese cities, increasingly, also in Africa (Gicha et al 2024, Noll et al 2026).

However, residual emissions will remain even under very high mitigation ambition. CDR technologies are thus a crucial component of net-zero strategies. Since CDR technologies tend to be landintensive (Smith et al 2015) most CDR potential lies outside of urban areas. Intra-urban CDR options 365

include urban trees and greening, wood-based construction, and biochar in construction materials; together, these options have been estimated to offer removal potential on the order of ~1 GtCO₂/yr globally (Rodriguez Mendez et al 2024).

Transport ● fleet electrification and charging infrastructure ● compact urban planning and transit-oriented development (Ewing and Cervero 2017, Nachtigall et al 2025) ● cycling and walking infrastructure (Creutzig et al 2022a, Millard-Ball et al 2025, Hinckson et al 2026, Kraus and Koch 2021)

Waste ● waste prevention (Möslinger et al 2023) ● organic waste diversion to avoid methane from landfills (Oo et al 2024) ● landfill methane capture (Oo et al., 2024)

Industry ● steel recycling (Onesmo et al 2024, Wu et al 2025) ● low-carbon cement (e.g.,with biochar) and wood-based construction (Chen et al 2023)

Energy supply ● renewables (rooftop & balcony PV in cities) (Galvin 2026, Zhang et al 2025) ● dynamic pricing and battery storage

CDR ● urban trees (Rodriguez Mendez et al 2024) ● biochar for buildings (Rodriguez Mendez et al 2024) ● wood-based construction (Mishra et al 2022) ● waste incineration with carbon capture and storage (Struthers et al 2022)

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. The downscaling approach assumes that sectoral emission-intensity reductions in urban areas follow national trends, which may not capture differences in transition dynamics between urban and rural areas. The 375

delineation of urban areas based on gridded population and GDP introduces uncertainty regarding the urban classification. Using administrative boundaries rather than only urban grid cells would result in a higher urban share of emissions, because emissions from non-populated areas within municipalities would also be included. In addition, the focus on territorial emissions excludes emissions embodied in traded goods, such as imported food or electricity, and therefore does not 380

capture the full carbon footprint of urban consumption. Finally, uncertainties inherent to IAM scenarios propagate into the urban emission estimates.

Future research could improve understanding of urban emission futures by representing subnational heterogeneity more explicitly, for example by distinguishing urban, rural, and interurban travel in assessments of mobility transitions and by capturing differences in building stocks and energy 385

demand between urban and rural areas. Accounting for the effects of urban planning on energy demand and related greenhouse gas emissions in scenario modeling would further improve the representation of mitigation options specific to cities. Machine learning could facilitate deeper integration of scenario projections with historical emission inventories and other data sources, such as mobility data, satellite imagery, and climate data, thereby improving the spatial downscaling of 390

future GHG emissions.

In conclusion, cities are central to achieving deep emission reductions. Realizing the urban mitigation potential requires rapid transformations in the energy supply, industry, buildings, transportation and waste sectors. Urban planning is a central lever to achieving mitigation across building and transport sectors. At the same time, the uneven distribution of emissions and mitigation potential across 395

regions and city types highlights the importance of differentiated, forward-looking strategies. Integrating spatially explicit urban insights into global scenario analysis provides a critical bridge between global climate targets and subnational climate action.

## Abstract

High-emissions scenarios explore the high end of climate risk assessment. However, the characteristics

of that high end have changed as clean-energy costs have declined and deployment has accelerated.

Here we document the Global Change Analysis Model (GCAM) contribution to ScenarioMIP for CMIP7,

focusing on the SSP3-based High emission scenario (H3), selected as the CMIP7 high-emissions marker.

H3 combines the SSP3 Regional Rivalry storyline with sustained climate-policy rollback in a fragmented

world, where slow technology diffusion, weak institutions, high population growth and continued fossil-

fuel reliance keep emissions rising through the century. Solar and wind still expand because cost

declines sustain deployment even under rollback, but too slowly to displace fossil fuels. Comparison

with a vetted scenario database, recent probabilistic projections and the ScenarioMIP High ensemble

places H3 toward the upper end of plausible emissions pathways. By 2100, H3 reaches approximately 76

Gt CO2-eq yr⁻¹ of Kyoto greenhouse-gas emissions and 53 Gt CO2 yr⁻¹ of energy and industrial CO2,

yielding median effective radiative forcing of about 6.5 W/m² and median warming of 3.4°C. An SSP5-

based high scenario (H5) shows that comparable high forcing can emerge through distinct

socioeconomic routes. H3 is selected as the CMIP7 marker because it directly pairs high warming with

SSP3's high challenges to adaptation; downstream applications can explore alternative socioeconomic

pairings. H3 forcing and warming outcomes are below the CMIP6-era SSP3 reference used here, and

## 1. Introduction

ScenarioMIP, the scenario component of the seventh Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP7),

changes how climate scenarios are organized. CMIP6 combined radiative-forcing outcomes with

socioeconomic narratives in the SSP-RCP framework (van Vuuren et al., 2014). CMIP7 is emissions-driven

and structured around policy narratives (van Vuuren et al., 2026), including continuation of current

policy (Medium emission), policy failure and fragmentation (High emission), and successful

implementation of Paris-aligned ambition (Low and Very Low emission scenarios). Radiative forcing and

warming are therefore outcomes of the emissions pathways rather than design targets.

High-emissions scenarios are used to investigate low-probability, high-consequence climate outcomes

(Kemp et al., 2022). RCP8.5 (Riahi et al., 2011) and SSP5-8.5 (Kriegler et al., 2017) served this role in

previous CMIP phases, with end-of-century warming near the high end of the assessed range. Their

frequent interpretation as likely or business-as-usual futures subsequently generated a broad plausibility

debate (Hausfather and Peters, 2020). Recent syntheses place central current-policy warming below 3°C

(Hausfather, 2025). A contemporary High scenario therefore serves a more specific purpose: exploring a

plausible high-end outcome that lies clearly above central expectations.

ScenarioMIP is designed to span emissions from the highest to the lowest plausible outcomes, where

plausibility reflects a unified judgement of non-negligible likelihood supported by multiple lines of

evidence (van Vuuren et al., 2026). The two ends of the range face different constraints. Low-emissions

pathways can be assessed against engineering feasibility and observed technology performance. At the

high end, sustained policy failure and path dependence must remain consistent with trajectories of

energy demand, land use and technology deployment over the century. Contemporary clean-energy

deployment also narrows the set of high-emissions energy systems that can be motivated from current

conditions.

The socioeconomic route to high forcing matters as well as the forcing level itself. H3 and H5 provide

two internally consistent examples: SSP3 reaches high forcing through fragmented, slow development

with high population and persistent energy and carbon intensities, whereas SSP5 reaches comparable

## 2. GCAM and scenario implementation

Each ScenarioMIP narrative is implemented in GCAM as a set of socioeconomic, policy, technology, and

land-use assumptions, resulting in internally consistent emissions, energy, land, and climate-relevant

pathways. For the High scenario, an extended rollback narrative was developed to support the

plausibility assessment in Section 4.

The eight scenarios adhere to the CMIP7 ScenarioMIP multi-model design, spanning emissions from

High to Very Low (van Vuuren et al., 2026). Their SSP foundations and defining assumptions are detailed

in Section 2.2.

### 2.1 GCAM framework

The Global Change Analysis Model (GCAM) is an open-source, technology-rich integrated assessment

model of coupled energy, water, agricultural, land-use, economic and climate systems (Calvin et al.,

2019; Gambhir et al., 2022). It is a dynamic-recursive partial-equilibrium model: at each time step, it

clears individual commodity markets for fuels, electricity, agricultural products, water and emissions

permits. Economy-wide equilibrium and intertemporal optimization are outside the model formulation.

Agents act without foresight, solving one period at a time from current prices and inherited capital

stocks. Technology choice follows a logit formulation in which market shares respond to relative costs.

Population and GDP enter exogenously, and the optional macroeconomic feedback module is disabled,

so each SSP's socioeconomic trajectory is held fixed across the suite. GCAM resolves 32 geopolitical

regions, 384 land-use regions and 235 water basins, with historical calibration through 2021 and five-

year projection periods from 2025 to 2100. Although 2021 is GCAM's final historical calibration year,

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Energy system

H3 and H5 reach high emissions through sharply different energy systems (Figure 1). From 2025 to 2100,

global primary energy in H3 increases by about 50%, from approximately 625 to 929 EJ yr⁻¹, while energy

intensity of GDP improves at only about 0.5% yr⁻¹. H5 expands much more strongly, reaching

approximately 1,340 EJ yr⁻¹ in 2100, with energy intensity improving at about 1.35% yr⁻¹. The recent

historical rate lies between these trajectories: on the same GDP convention, global energy intensity

improved at about 1.15% per year between 2005 and 2020, so H3 improves at less than half the

historical pace while H5 slightly exceeds it. The larger H5 system therefore supports greater absolute

fossil-energy use and higher energy and industrial CO2 emissions, even as its energy mix changes more

quickly. Regional and full-century energy-system results are provided in SI Sections S6 and S7.

Absolute coal use is similar in H3 and H5 over much of the century, but coal remains close to one

quarter of H3 primary energy throughout, at 27% in 2100, compared with 16% in H5. No climate-policy

pressure drives this divergence in either High scenario. Slower substitution under SSP3 keeps coal

structurally entrenched in the smaller H3 energy system, whereas faster technological progress and

stronger substitution toward alternatives reduce coal's share in the much larger H5 system.

The stable aggregate share in H3 masks a shift in coal use across sectors. Industrial coal drives the first

half of the century, rising from 50 to 70 EJ per year by 2050 before plateauing, with growth

concentrated in light manufacturing rather than iron and steel, where coal use declines throughout.

Electricity demand grows by about 40% while coal generation rises by 65%, lifting coal's share of

generation from a mid-century trough of 22% to 26% in 2100 and raising power-sector coal use from 41

to 68 EJ yr⁻¹. Coal capacity expands accordingly and remains unabated. H3 is the only scenario in the

suite that holds coal near a quarter of both electricity generation and industrial final energy through

2100; in M, the corresponding shares fall to 6% and 15% (SI Section S3.3; Figure S3.3.4). Electrification

also proceeds more slowly in H3. The electric share of light-duty vehicles rises from about 8% in 2025 to

only one third by 2100, while wind and solar increase from about 22% to 39% of electricity through cost-

driven deployment (SI Figure S11.4).

### 3.2 Land use

Cropland in H3 expands by more than 30% over the century (from approximately 1620 to 2130 Mha),

primarily to feed a population approaching 13 billion (Figure 2a). Land-use CO2 remains positive

throughout but declines after mid-century as deforestation slows (Figure 3d). Purpose-grown bioenergy

accounts for about one-third of new cropland by 2100 and responds to energy demand rather than

climate policy; with little carbon-price incentive for removals, large-scale BECCS does not emerge. Forest

trajectories are shown in Figure 2b; full land-use transitions are in SI Section S9.

### 3.3 Emissions trajectories

The energy- and land-system responses produce strongly differentiated emissions pathways. In H3,

global Kyoto greenhouse-gas emissions rise from approximately 52 Gt CO2-eq yr⁻¹ in 2020 to 76 Gt CO2-

eq yr⁻¹ in 2100, while energy and industrial CO2 emissions increase from 35 to 53 Gt CO2 yr⁻¹ (Figure

3a,b). Neither trajectory peaks before 2100 because policy rollback persists through the century. H5 also

rises monotonically, supported by its much larger SSP5 energy system.

H3 and H5 reach broadly similar Kyoto GHG totals through different emissions compositions. H3 has

lower energy and industrial CO2 because economic activity and the energy system are smaller, but

higher land-use CO2 and methane. Total CH4 reaches approximately 528 Mt CH4 yr⁻¹ in H3 in 2100,

compared with 400 Mt CH4 yr⁻¹ in H5. The H3 methane burden reflects its larger population (and

therefore food demand) and slower diffusion of methane-reducing technologies and practices under

SSP3 conditions; the sectoral decomposition is reported in SI Section S8.

The other six scenarios span progressively lower emissions. HL5 follows H5 through mid-century, then

declines sharply as policy shifts toward net zero CO2, crossing into net-negative CO2 emissions near

2100. M continues current policy, with CO2 falling only modestly, from 37 Gt in 2050 to 32 Gt in 2100.

ML holds current trends to 2040 before declining to roughly net-zero CO2 by 2100. L follows near-term

NDCs and reaches net-zero CO2 around 2070. LN and VL1 both reach net-zero CO2 around 2060 and

CO2 emissions are net-negative thereafter: LN through delayed action followed by heavy removal, and

VL1 through early SSP1-based mitigation. Cumulative 2025 to 2100 CO2 falls across the suite, from 3700

Gt in H3 to under 300 Gt in the Very Low scenarios. In the net-negative pathways, the running total

peaks well above its 2100 value, reaching 690 Gt in LN and 480 Gt in VL1; this peak governs maximum

### 3.4 Carbon dioxide removal

CDR in H3 and H5 is minimal across all technologies, reaching 0.4 and 1.2 Gt CO2 yr⁻¹ in 2100,

respectively, because GCAM deploys removal in response to carbon pricing and carbon prices in these

scenarios approach zero (SI Section S13). Deployment across the rest of the suite scales with the depth

and timing of the required reductions. Gross removal in 2100 reaches 1.6 Gt CO2 yr⁻¹ in M, 6.7 in ML, 8.2

in L and 8.0 in VL1. The sharpest late-century deployment occurs in HL5 and LN, at 19.8 and 18.2 Gt CO2

yr⁻¹, respectively: HL5 uses large-scale removal to reverse a high mid-century peak, while LN relies

heavily on BECCS and direct air capture after delayed near-term action. VL1 reaches a similar low-

emissions endpoint with less removal because early SSP1 mitigation and demand-side changes lower the

burden on CDR (SI Section S10).

### 3.5 Climate outcomes

ScenarioMIP marker scenarios, including H3, are being run by Earth system models to project climate

outcomes with the latest model versions. GCAM emissions scenarios, together with the other

ScenarioMIP submissions, have also been assessed with the reduced-complexity climate model MAGICC

v7.6.0a3 to provide preliminary forcing and warming estimates with probabilistic uncertainty ranges

(Nicholls et al., 2025). Unless stated otherwise, the forcing and warming values reported in this paper

are medians from that assessment. H5 is the warmest GCAM pathway, with median effective radiative

forcing of approximately 7.0 W/m² and median warming of 3.7°C in 2100; H3 reaches approximately 6.5

W/m² and 3.4°C. The remaining scenarios step down progressively with mitigation stringency toward

the Low and Very Low pathways (Figure 4). The H3 uncertainty distribution extends to approximately

4.8°C in 2100 at the 95th percentile. Cumulative emissions and the corresponding climate outcomes for

all eight scenarios are given in Table 3.

Gross greenhouse-gas forcing in H3 is close to 7.0 W/m² in 2100, while aerosol cooling offsets roughly

0.9 W/m² and tropospheric ozone adds about 0.5 W/m², yielding net effective radiative forcing of 6.5

W/m². H3 retains the deepest aerosol cooling in the suite because air-quality controls remain weak

under SSP3 fragmentation. H5 has a larger fossil-energy system but stronger pollution control under

SSP5, producing a smaller aerosol offset. The decomposition by forcing agent and the corresponding

aerosol-precursor emissions are reported in SI Section S8.

## 4. High scenario marker: selection and plausibility

### 4.1 Marker selection: H3 and H5

H3 and H5 are both internally consistent High emission scenarios and are treated here as equally

plausible. They reach similar end-of-century forcing through different socioeconomic systems and

emissions compositions (Section 3). Marker selection therefore turns on the socioeconomic context

encoded natively in the scenario used widely for downstream climate-impact applications.


<!-- Page 13 -->


13

Persistent fragmentation and slow development leave projected per-capita income near 14,000 USD

(2010) in H3 in 2100, compared with about 66,000 USD in H5, while both scenarios maintain high

emissions and warming. H3 and H5 therefore show that high forcing remains compatible with distinct

development routes: fragmented, low-growth SSP3 conditions and fossil-fuel-intensive, high-growth

SSP5 conditions. The GCAM suite retains both routes to the high end of the emissions range, with H5

available explicitly for applications centred on the SSP5 context. Additional development and energy-

access indicators are reported in SI Section S11.

For impacts research, H3 directly pairs high warming with SSP3's high challenges to adaptation, a

particularly risk-relevant combination (Simpson et al., 2021). The scenario-matrix framework also

permits downstream applications to combine climate outcomes with alternative socioeconomic

pathways, including higher-capacity contexts (van Vuuren et al., 2014). H3 is selected to make the high-

warming, high-adaptation-challenge case available in the core marker set while preserving broader

socioeconomic interpretations.

The emissions-composition differences documented in Section 3 broaden the range of high-forcing

mechanisms represented by the two GCAM High scenarios: H3 carries more land-use CO2 and methane,

whereas H5 carries more fossil and industrial CO2. These differences follow from the socioeconomic

pathways and help characterize the alternatives; the marker selection itself rests on the downstream

value of the native socioeconomic pairing.

### 4.2 H3 as a plausible high-emissions pathway

The ScenarioMIP experimental design calls for the High emission scenario to represent emissions that

are 'as high as plausible' (van Vuuren et al., 2026). We interpret this as a high-end pathway with non-

negligible likelihood supported by multiple lines of evidence. H3 occupies that high end while leaving

room for more extreme cases that require additional assumptions beyond the marker design.

H3 builds on SSP3 Regional Rivalry, a world of weak institutions, high population growth, slow and

uneven development, constrained trade and slow technology diffusion (O'Neill et al., 2017). GCAM

combines these socioeconomic conditions with sustained climate-policy rollback through four

mechanisms: institutional erosion, policy inconsistency, technology-deployment friction and carbon

lock-in. Their cumulative effect is a fragmented policy environment in which existing ambition erodes,

implementation remains uneven and fossil infrastructure persists without requiring coordinated global


<!-- Page 14 -->


14

abandonment of climate action. SI Sections S3.1 and S3.2 develop the narrative and its grounding in the

policy-failure literature.

Contemporary energy-system conditions also constrain the pathway. Solar and wind supplied more than

17% of global electricity in 2025, up from about 10% in 2019, and cost competitiveness increasingly

supports deployment even where climate policy is weak (Ember, 2026; IRENA, 2024). H3 therefore

retains adoption of renewables and electric vehicles where they are economically attractive.

Fragmentation, low investment and deployment frictions slow the transition enough to keep fossil fuels

dominant, combining continued clean-technology progress with deployment too slow to displace the

incumbent fossil system (SI Section S4).

## 5. Comparison with CMIP6 scenarios

AIM/CGE 2.0 SSP3-Baseline provides the Regional Rivalry benchmark for the CMIP6 comparison, while

REMIND-MAgPIE SSP5-Baseline represents SSP5-8.5, the pathway that dominated the CMIP6 plausibility

debate (Pielke et al., 2022; Hausfather and Peters, 2020; Hausfather, 2025).

Relative to the CMIP6 SSP3 comparator, H3 reaches lower end-of-century emissions, forcing and

warming. Effective radiative forcing falls from approximately 7.6 to 6.5 W/m². Several changes coincide

with this divergence: renewable and electric-vehicle costs now incorporate observed declines, coal

assumptions reflect the post-2014 global plateau, the base year has advanced to 2021, and the SSP3

population and GDP projections have been updated (K.C. et al., 2024; Dellink et al., 2025). These

changes occur together, so their individual contributions are not isolated here.

The energy systems increasingly diverge over the century (Figure 7). By 2100, primary energy from coal

in H3 is less than half the level in the CMIP6-era SSP3 comparator and total primary energy is nearly 25%

lower. Cumulative fossil and industrial CO2 over 2020 to 2100 is approximately 29% lower in H3, with

fossil and industrial CO2 accounting for most of the century-scale GHG difference. The climate emulators

used for the two scenario generations also differ, so forcing values are best interpreted as approximate

comparators; the direction of change is robust (SI Section S5).

Against SSP5-8.5, H3 has substantially lower fossil and industrial CO2, lower coal use and lower end-of-

century forcing, while retaining more clean-technology deployment. Contemporary high pathways

therefore do not reproduce the scale of fossil expansion embedded in the CMIP6 high-end pathway.

Additional compositional diagnostics for both CMIP6 comparators are reported in SI Section S5.

## 6. Discussion

### 6.1 Implications for climate risk assessment

H3 changes the framing of high-end climate risk along two dimensions. Its end-of-century forcing is

lower than in the CMIP6 high-end scenarios, reducing the physical hazard sampled by the marker. At the

same time, its SSP3 foundation carries high challenges to adaptation through slower development and

weaker institutions. The marker therefore makes a high-warming, high-adaptation-challenge

combination directly available to impacts research. The net effect on assessed risk will vary across

impact domains according to the relative importance of hazard, exposure and adaptive capacity.

The SSP3 basis is a choice about which risks the marker keeps visible, and it carries no claim about

where responsibility for high emissions lies. H3's emissions arise from persistent carbon intensity and

sustained policy failure in a fragmented world; per-capita emissions under SSP3 remain modest, and the

pathway does not attribute the high-emissions future to the consumption of lower-income populations.

Pairing high warming only with a wealthy socioeconomic context, as SSP5-8.5 did, would build the

affordability of adaptation into the marker itself and understate risks to the populations with the least

capacity to adapt. The SSP3 pairing keeps those populations in the frame for impacts research.

H5 preserves an explicit alternative route to high-end warming in a much wealthier SSP5 world, so the

scenario set does not equate high warming with low income. Downstream studies can also combine H3

climate outcomes with alternative SSPs where the scenario-matrix architecture permits. The marker

choice therefore highlights one risk-relevant native pairing while preserving a broader socioeconomic

scenario space for impacts applications.

### 6.2 Technology momentum at the high end of the emissions range

Clean-technology momentum now shapes the high end of the emissions range as well as mitigation

pathways. In H3, solar, wind and electric vehicles continue to gain market share under sustained climate

policy rollback, with wind and solar approaching 40% of electricity by 2100. High emissions persist

because deployment remains too slow to displace the inherited fossil system under fragmentation and

weak policy. This produces a different high-end energy system from the coal-intensive pathways used in

earlier scenario generations and shifts attention toward the persistence of institutional, investment and

deployment constraints in an energy system already undergoing technological change.

### 6.3 Limitations

H3 represents one internally consistent route to high emissions in a fragmented world. H5 demonstrates

another route through high-growth SSP5 conditions, and still other configurations could produce similar

or higher forcing through different compositions. The narrative, consistency check and external

benchmarks in Section 4 position H3 toward the plausible high end but do not establish a numerical

ceiling. More extreme scenarios remain necessary for questions that require outcomes beyond the

ScenarioMIP marker range.

GCAM treats the political economy of rollback as an exogenous scenario condition. Policy assumptions

enter through regionally differentiated carbon prices, technology cost paths and deployment constraints

(Section 2.2; SI Section S2), and the same governance weaknesses that suppress mitigation also bind

CDR deployment. Endogenizing interactions among policy, incumbent interests, electoral cycles and

public opinion would provide a complementary extension.

Regional detail is limited by GCAM’s 32-region structure, which aggregates within-region heterogeneity

in transition capacity, institutional quality and resource endowment. The regional patterns in Section 3.1

and SI Section S6 should be read as plausible realizations of differential policy failure across region

groups and should not be interpreted as country-level projections.

## 7. Conclusion

H3 reflects a changed high-emissions landscape. Clean technologies continue to improve and diffuse

even under sustained climate-policy rollback, constraining the fossil expansion that characterized earlier

high-end scenarios. Yet slower substitution, persistent fossil infrastructure and fragmented institutions

are sufficient to keep emissions rising through the century, producing a median warming of 3.4°C by

2100. H5 demonstrates that a similar level of warming can emerge through a very different, high-growth

SSP5 pathway; together, the two scenarios show that the contemporary high-emissions range spans

distinct socioeconomic routes rather than a single archetype of fossil-intensive development. Selecting

H3 as the CMIP7 marker makes one particularly consequential combination directly available for

climate-risk research: substantial warming alongside the high challenges to adaptation of SSP3. The

broader scenario framework retains alternative socioeconomic pairings, allowing downstream studies to

explore how the consequences of high warming vary with the societies exposed to it.

S1 GCAM framework and ScenarioMIP updates

The ScenarioMIP contribution uses GCAM 8s, a ScenarioMIP-specific branch based on GCAM 8.1 with

ScenarioMIP. Its main structural difference from public GCAM 8.2 is regional aggregation. GCAM 8.2

separates Ukraine from the former Europe_Eastern region to reflect geopolitical developments since

2022; GCAM 8s retains the 32-region structure used in GCAM 8.1 and earlier releases. The remaining

structural differences are documented below. The closest public reference for model code and input

data is the GCAM 8.2 Zenodo release (JGCRI, 2025a), with documentation in the companion record

S1.1 GCAM overview

GCAM is an open-source, technology-rich integrated assessment model of coupled energy, water,

agricultural, land-use, economic and climate systems (Calvin et al., 2019; Gambhir et al., 2022). It is a

dynamic-recursive partial-equilibrium model. At each five-year time step, GCAM clears markets for fuels,

electricity, agricultural products, water and emissions permits; economy-wide equilibrium and full-

horizon optimization are outside the model formulation. Agents act without foresight, solving one

period from current prices and inherited stocks before carrying resource depletion, capital-stock

changes and landscape modifications into the next. Technology choice follows a logit formulation in

which market shares respond to relative costs. Population and GDP per capita are prescribed

exogenously from the SSP framework. The optional MACRO feedback module is disabled, so GDP

regions and 235 water basins, with historical calibration in 2019, 2020 and 2021. Hector is used

internally as a reduced-form carbon-cycle and climate model; the temperature outcomes reported here

come from MAGICC driven by GCAM emissions, consistent with the ScenarioMIP framework.

S3 Extended H3 scenario narrative: foundations and mechanisms of policy rollback

The H trajectory combines SSP3 fragmentation with sustained policy rollback through four mechanisms:

institutional erosion, policy inconsistency, technology-deployment friction and fossil-fuel persistence

through carbon lock-in.

S3.1 Narrative foundations and mechanisms of policy rollback

S3.1.1 Narrative foundations

The H marker narrative starts from the SSP3 "Regional Rivalry" storyline (O'Neill et al., 2017), updated

for contemporary climate governance and domestic climate politics. SSP3 describes a fragmented world

with resurgent nationalism, weak global institutions, high population growth in developing regions, and

slow, uneven economic and technological development. It combines high mitigation and adaptation

challenges: the institutional weaknesses that impede coordinated decarbonization also constrain

investment in climate-resilient infrastructure, early-warning systems and social protection. The storyline

has antecedents in SRES A2 (Nakicenovic et al., 2000) and in the MESSAGE A2r pathway, a revised A2

implementation developed in the 2000s (Riahi et al., 2007). That high-emissions lineage subsequently

fed into RCP8.5 (Riahi et al., 2011), although H3 is constructed from the SSP3 framework rather than by

extending the older RCP pathway.

The climate-governance basis for the H scenario draws on scholarship that treats international climate

policy as a regime complex, with overlapping institutions rather than a single integrated framework

(Keohane and Victor, 2011). Victor (2011) links the failure of the 2009 Copenhagen Summit's top-down

negotiation model to the decentralized architecture of the Paris Agreement, where national

commitments replace binding international targets. Paris was designed to build ambition through

successive rounds of stronger nationally determined contributions. In the H scenario, that ratchet stalls.

Formal climate agreements persist, but enforcement capacity and political durability weaken;

commitments are not strengthened on schedule; and the implementation gap between stated ambition

and actual emissions widens.

The global economic context reinforces this governance setting. The IMF (2023) warns that

geoeconomic fragmentation, including the decoupling of major economies into rival trade and

technology blocs, could slow the cross-border diffusion of low-carbon technologies and hamper

decarbonization. The H narrative treats such fragmentation as a persistent structural condition across

the modelling horizon. This assumption is stronger than would be used for near-term policy analysis. The


<!-- Page 32 -->


8

scenario should therefore be read as a stress test of sustained fragmentation and its emissions

consequences, not as a central forecast.

S3.1.2 Four mechanisms of policy rollback

Within the SSP3 fragmentation context, the H scenario envisions sustained climate-policy rollback

through four mutually reinforcing mechanisms. Institutional erosion weakens the international

coordination that would discipline national reversals. Policy inconsistency within countries compounds

this erosion. Technology-deployment friction slows the displacement of fossil infrastructure. Carbon

lock-in sustains demand for incumbent fossil systems even as alternatives improve. The mechanisms are

analytically separable, but their emissions effect arises from their interaction.

Institutional erosion

Institutional erosion is the progressive weakening of the international institutions and coordination

frameworks that support climate action. In the H narrative, major economies increasingly prioritize

domestic concerns, appetite for binding international commitments declines, and trade tensions,

geopolitical competition and nationalist politics reduce the space for climate diplomacy. Climate

agreements may persist formally while losing the enforcement mechanisms and political support

needed to drive emissions reductions. The Paris ratchet mechanism, which depends on repeated

strengthening of commitments, stalls.

The erosion is regionally uneven. Some countries maintain nominal climate commitments and may

initially strengthen rhetoric, while others roll back commitments or fail to implement them. The shared

institutional foundation for ambitious climate action weakens even without universal withdrawal from

the Paris framework. The IMF's 2023 analysis of geoeconomic fragmentation provides one empirical

anchor, showing how decoupling in trade and technology can slow cross-border mitigation-technology

diffusion and make coordinated ambition harder to sustain. In the H scenario, these dynamics persist

long enough for the institutional fabric of climate cooperation to thin over the century.

Policy inconsistency

Policy inconsistency operates within countries through policy reversal, uneven implementation and the

failure to sustain ambition across electoral cycles and administrative transitions. In the H narrative,

climate policies are adopted unevenly and then weakened when governments change, administrative

capacity falls short, or incumbent interests mobilize. Stokes (2020) shows how electric utilities in the

United States used political influence to weaken renewable portfolio standards, demonstrating that

incumbent opposition can produce policy stagnation even in favourable political settings. The H scenario


<!-- Page 33 -->


9

generalizes this dynamic across regions and policy domains where climate policy threatens established

energy interests.

The policy-studies literature treats failure as a matter of degree. Sokołowski and Heffron (2022) define

energy policy failure as a policy falling short of societal goals in the energy and climate domain,

especially emissions, security and justice goals. McConnell (2016) emphasizes that policies can succeed

and fail along different dimensions, and that political narratives shape the perception of failure. The H

scenario adopts this graded view. Carbon-pricing regimes are introduced and then weakened or

abandoned at different rates across regions; renewable mandates face sustained but uneven opposition;

and the resulting policy landscape is fragmented and inconsistent. Meckling et al. (2015) argue that

policy durability depends on coalitions that survive electoral cycles; the H scenario represents a world in

which such coalitions either fail to form or cannot withstand incumbent opposition.

Technology deployment friction

Technology-deployment friction concerns the pace at which clean technologies scale once they are

technically available and economically competitive. In the H narrative, clean technologies continue to

improve and deploy, but deployment remains well below its technical and economic potential. The

scenario includes a deployment floor from cost-driven solar, wind and electric vehicles, reaching

approximately 40 percent of electricity generation by 2100. The ceiling remains lower than in favourable

policy environments because several frictions bind simultaneously: grid integration limits variable

renewable absorption; permitting delays slow projects; land-use conflicts constrain siting; skilled-labour

bottlenecks slow installation; and fragmented critical-mineral supply chains impede technology

diffusion.

Carley and Konisky (2020) show that energy transitions create winners and losers, and that backlash

over perceived distributional injustice can derail policy support even when a transition is economically

beneficial in aggregate. In the H scenario, these frictions become widespread and persistent. Local

opposition to clean-energy infrastructure, distributional concerns about transition costs and unequal

access to transition benefits all slow deployment. Clean technologies continue to improve and spread;

the binding constraint is the rate at which institutions can resolve the frictions around deployment. In

the H world, that rate lags behind energy-demand growth and fossil-infrastructure replacement.

Fossil fuel persistence through carbon lock-in

Fossil infrastructure can persist through path dependence as well as deliberate policy support. Unruh

(2000) describes carbon lock-in as the self-perpetuating inertia of fossil-based infrastructure, institutions


<!-- Page 34 -->


10

and behaviours that sustains fossil dependence even when cleaner alternatives are technically available

and economically attractive. Seto et al. (2016) identify three simultaneous forms. Infrastructural lock-in

keeps fossil generation capacity, internal-combustion vehicle fleets and fossil-based industrial processes

operating to the end of life. Institutional lock-in resides in governance structures, regulatory frameworks

and political coalitions that protect fossil interests. Behavioural lock-in reflects consumption patterns,

preferences and demand structures that change slowly without strong price or convenience signals.

In the H scenario, these forms of lock-in interact to sustain fossil dependence even as cleaner

alternatives become cheaper. Existing fossil infrastructure operates to the end of its life because early

retirement lacks institutional and regulatory support. New fossil investments continue in regions where

alternatives face the deployment frictions described above. Energy-security concerns, especially in

regions with domestic fossil resources, further support extraction and consumption. Fossil fuels retain

market share through many locally rational infrastructure, institutional and behavioural decisions that

collectively produce a high-emissions trajectory.

Tong et al. (2019) quantify the cumulative-emissions implications of existing fossil infrastructure,

showing that plants and facilities already operating or under construction could exhaust the carbon

budget compatible with limiting warming to 1.5°C. The H scenario adds new fossil capacity in regions

where alternatives face barriers, compounding these committed emissions. The Production Gap

literature provides further empirical grounding: SEI et al. (2021) document that major fossil-fuel-

producing nations maintain 2030 production plans roughly double the levels compatible with 1.5°C

pathways, and Erickson et al. (2015) analyze how government support for fossil extraction undermines

stated climate goals. These production plans and subsidies are not formal climate-policy rollbacks, but

they are features of the incumbent energy system that persist under the H narrative.

S3.2 Scope of the policy-failure assumption

We use policy failure in a bounded sense: partial, uneven and cumulative underperformance against

stated climate and energy goals (Sokołowski and Heffron, 2022; McConnell, 2016). Climate policy

remains present in the H scenario, but ambition erodes, implementation becomes less durable and

coordination weakens across regions.

The boundary is deliberately conservative: climate policy persists in some regions; reversals occur at

different times; fossil-fuel support remains heterogeneous; and climate denial is not assumed to

dominate major economies. Within those bounds, ambition erodes gradually, the Paris ratchet stalls,

regional trajectories diverge and deployment frictions persist.


<!-- Page 35 -->


11

The Production Gap literature shows persistent gaps between stated climate goals and fossil-extraction

plans in major producing nations (SEI et al., 2021; Erickson et al., 2015), indicating incomplete political

conditions for coordinated fossil phase-out even in some countries with ambitious stated climate

policies. Stokes (2020) documents incumbent opposition to renewable-energy mandates in the United

States through ordinary political channels, and Carley and Konisky (2020) identify distributional concerns

about transition costs as a source of backlash against clean-energy policy. No single case establishes a

century-scale H trajectory; collectively, they identify mechanisms through which incremental reversals,

uneven implementation and sustained deployment friction can accumulate into persistent policy

underperformance.

H3 combines partial, inconsistent and fragmented climate action. Momentum from the early-2020s

energy transition slows without disappearing: some regions continue clean-energy deployment on

economic grounds while others roll back policy support, and formal commitments persist while

ratcheting fails in practice. The trajectory reaches the high end of the plausible high-emissions space as

one internally consistent route to substantial end-of-century warming under sustained fragmentation

and rollback.

S3.3 Coal trajectories across high-emissions scenarios

Coal use provides a useful plausibility test because critiques of earlier high-end scenarios focused in part

on renewed coal expansion. H3 and H5 remain within reserve-scale cumulative use and within the

ScenarioMIP High ensemble; the comparisons below separate reserve and resource accounting from

multi-model coal trajectories. Marker selection itself rests on the socioeconomic pairing described in

Section S4.3.

S3.3.1 Observed coal dynamics and the literature critique

Global coal consumption shifted from rapid growth to a broad plateau in the mid-2010s, with

subsequent year-to-year variation driven by economic cycles, weather and fuel prices (IEA, 2024). The

shift followed roughly two decades of rapid demand growth led by coal-fired electricity and

industrialization in China and other fast-growing Asian economies. Future coal use could depart from

this plateau, but scenarios requiring a sustained return to very rapid global expansion face a higher

evidentiary burden.

Coal-supply terminology is important in interpreting long-term scenarios. Proven reserves are quantities

known to be economically recoverable under current technical and economic conditions; resources are

broader estimates of coal in place or potentially recoverable and can exceed current reserves


<!-- Page 36 -->


12

substantially. A century-scale scenario can therefore use more coal than today's proven reserves

without being physically impossible, because prices, technology and exploration can move resources

into the reserve category over time. Earlier critiques of RCP8.5 and SSP5-8.5 accordingly concern more

than reserve accounting: they also emphasize the scale of renewed coal-plant construction, the

economics of coal relative to alternatives, and the expansion of coal-intensive conversion sectors such

as coal-to-liquids (Ritchie and Dowlatabadi, 2017). Reserve and resource benchmarks in Figure S3.3.1

follow GEA (2012) and Bauer et al. (2016) for proven reserves, Mohr et al. (2015) for recoverable

resources, and Rogner et al. (2012) for coal in place.

Recent assessments of current-policy and plausible-baseline scenarios reinforce the importance of these

system dynamics. Hausfather and Peters (2020) argue that treating RCP8.5 and SSP5-8.5 as business-as-

usual overstated support from observed trends, while Hausfather (2025) finds that current-policy

projections now place central 21st-century warming below 3°C and that SSP5-8.5-level pathways require

reversal of current policy and technology trends. The relevant constraint for H3 and H5 is therefore not

an assumption that coal supply is exhausted. It is whether a large and sustained coal expansion remains

economically and technologically coherent as alternatives continue to improve.

H3 and H5 each use about 16,500 EJ of coal cumulatively from 2020 to 2100, within the range

represented by current reserve estimates, while the CMIP6-era SSP3 and SSP5 references draw on

progressively larger portions of broader resource estimates (Figure S3.3.1). Coal supply is therefore not

the binding constraint in the GCAM High pathways; their more conservative cumulative use follows

primarily from the evolving economics and deployment of competing technologies.

S4 H3 and H5: detailed comparison and marker context

S4.1 GCAM implementation and trajectory differences

H3 and H5 use the same GCAM 8s architecture, clean-energy technology cost paths and climate-policy

rollback structure. They differ in socioeconomic foundation: H3 uses SSP3 population, GDP and

development trajectories, whereas H5 uses SSP5. Carbon-price phase-out, weakening of renewable

mandates and electric-vehicle policy constraints are implemented consistently across the two scenarios,

so the comparison primarily reflects differences in socioeconomic context rather than different policy

designs.

At identical clean-energy technology costs, the SSP context changes how technologies deploy. Air-

pollution governance is one important channel. SSP3 combines lower income with weaker and more

fragmented air-quality regulation, reducing the pollution-control costs attached to coal in H3 and

slowing substitution in some regions. H5 couples higher income to stronger environmental management

and faster technology turnover. These differences help explain the higher coal share and lower

renewable share in H3, as well as its larger aerosol-precursor emissions, even though H5 operates the

larger energy system.

H3 reaches a population of approximately 13.1 billion in 2100, compared with 8.2 billion in H5, while

the other.

S4.2 Clean-technology deployment as a contemporary constraint

Observed clean-energy deployment over the past decade constrains the energy-system combinations

that can coherently sustain very high emissions. Solar and wind generation rose from roughly 10% to

more than 17% of global electricity between 2019 and 2025 (Ember, 2026), and electric-vehicle sales

reached approximately 20% of global new-car sales in 2024 (IEA, 2025). H3 and H5 therefore retain

deployment of increasingly competitive clean technologies even as climate-policy support weakens, but

meet the remaining demand through different fossil and non-fossil mixes. Their emissions outcomes

emerge from these energy-system responses within the broader SSP conditions.

S4.3 Socioeconomic context and adaptive-capacity pairing

H3 and H5 are treated as equally plausible High pathways; their distinction lies in the socioeconomic

context paired natively with the climate outcome. SSP3 combines high challenges to mitigation and

adaptation, whereas SSP5 pairs high emissions with much higher incomes, education, health and

institutional capacity (O'Neill et al., 2017). H3 therefore makes high warming directly available with

SSP3's high adaptation challenges, while H5 provides the high-growth, high-capacity route to similar

forcing. Scenario-matrix applications can combine climate outcomes with alternative socioeconomic

conditions downstream (van Vuuren et al., 2014). The marker choice reflects the value of including the

high-warming, high-adaptation-challenge pairing in the core scenario set.
